extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, IP practitioners, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and evaluative criteria for assessing patent claim definiteness (35 U.S.C. §112(b)) in litigation, including sources to consult, burden of proof, and proper application of precedent (Nautilus, Phillips, Markman). Useful for construing claims and deciding indefiniteness at district and appellate levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for claim construction and indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is a question of law and receives de novo review on appeal; claim indefiniteness is a legal conclusion implementing 35 U.S.C. § 112, and is reviewed de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., 517 U.S. 370, 390–91 (1996); Teva Pharms. USA, Inc. v. Sandoz, Inc., 574 U.S. 318, 325 (2015); Atmel Corp. v. Info. Storage Devices, Inc., 198 F.3d 1374, 1378 (Fed. Cir. 1999) ('A determination of claim indefiniteness is a legal conclusion ...'). Courts should apply de novo review to the legal question of indefiniteness, while recognizing any subsidiary factual findings may have separate standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewpoint of a person skilled in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefiniteness is decided from the viewpoint of persons skilled in the field of the invention; claims must inform such persons about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example case-specific POSITA definition here: 'at least a master’s degree in computer science or a related field, or a bachelor’s degree ... plus two years of relevant experience, with experience in computer graphics, computer-aided design, solid modeling, or geometric modeling.' (District court agreed definition cited by parties.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: United States patents carry a presumption of validity under 35 U.S.C. § 282; a party asserting invalidity must prove it by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Sonix Tech. Co. v. Publ’ns Int’l, Ltd., 844 F.3d 1370, 1377 (Fed. Cir. 2017). Courts must account for this presumption when evaluating indefiniteness challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness requirement (Nautilus 'reasonable certainty' standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 112, claims, viewed in light of the specification and prosecution history, must inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty; the requirement mandates clarity but recognizes absolute precision is unattainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary authority: Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc., 572 U.S. 898, 910 (2014): 'inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.' Courts must read claims in context (intrinsic record) to assess reasonable certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper sources for claim construction: intrinsic and extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should look first to the intrinsic record—the words of the claims themselves, the remainder of the specification, and the prosecution history—and may consult extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, technical dictionaries, state of the art) to inform meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303, 1314 (Fed. Cir. 2005) (en banc). Extrinsic evidence can explain technical terms and the state of the art but does not override intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of claims versus specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the patent right and provide legal notice of the boundaries of the monopoly; the specification teaches and describes the invention. Claims need not duplicate the detailed technical description in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ariad Pharms., Inc. v. Eli Lilly & Co., 598 F.3d 1336, 1347 (Fed. Cir. 2010) ('Claims define and circumscribe, the written description discloses and teaches.'); In re Vamco Mach. & Tool, Inc., 752 F.2d 1564, 1577 n.5 (Fed. Cir. 1985) (claims are legal documents defining scope). Use specification to interpret claims, but claims remain the metes and bounds of the right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorrect 'unanswered questions' or 'claim language standing alone' test is an improper standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard that declares a claim indefinite if there exist any 'unanswered questions' or if alleged ambiguities are not resolved 'in the claim language, standing alone' is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must not require that every technical question raised by an expert be answered within the literal claim language; instead, claims are read in light of the specification and prosecution history to determine how a POSITA would understand them. The district court erred applying an 'unanswered questions' test in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of expert testimony in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony may be used to explain terms of art, the meaning of technical terms, and the state of the art, but it cannot be used to establish the proper or legal construction of the claim language itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Teva Pharms., 574 U.S. at 332 (quoting Winans v. N.Y. & Erie R.R. Co., 62 U.S. 88, 100–01 (1859)). Experts inform the factual record about technology; legal claim construction remains the court's task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and relevance of prosecution history and examiner amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history—including examiner rejections and applicant amendments resolving rejections—bears on claim meaning and definiteness; an examiner's withdrawal of an indefiniteness rejection after claim amendment is a relevant fact in construing claims and assessing indefiniteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: examiner initially rejected claims for indefiniteness and required specific amendments; applicant amended claims in consultation with examiner and the examiner withdrew the indefiniteness rejection and allowed the claims. Courts should consider such prosecution events rather than ignoring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art and established approaches can inform definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the general approach is sufficiently well established in the art and referenced in the patent (e.g., Watson and Delaunay methods), that background can render claim language definite because a POSITA would understand the claimed improvement in that context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Presidio Components, Inc. v. Am. Tech. Ceramics Corp., 875 F.3d 1369, 1377 (Fed. Cir. 2017). Use of well-known prior art in the specification and claims may clarify terms that otherwise appear terse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty required: reasonable, not absolute; patents addressed to skilled artisans
rubrics_metrics.description: The definiteness requirement demands clarity sufficient to apprise skilled artisans of the claimed scope with reasonable certainty; it does not require absolute precision in all cases and patents are addressed to those skilled in the art (not the general public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Nautilus, 572 U.S. at 909–10; Carnegie Steel Co. v. Cambria Iron Co., 185 U.S. 403, 437 (1902). Courts should balance competing concerns and apply a standard of reasonableness in light of the subject matter.
